where: the estate on the swamp road north of Blackrose
what: Rows-For-Another took a boat from the estate's stores on an Owing of four months' work, as the estate's people still take boats; the estate assessed it in its own book.
The steward wrote into the book what she ate, the boat's upkeep and the sick days, each line true, and the Owing grew faster than she worked it; she has grown grey from years away from her tree.
Never-Sold has heard of the woman and has put by enough to buy out what the Owing was, not what the book says.
Two estate men walk the landing at night; the channel runs from the landing out of the estate's reach, and an Argonian cannot drown.

where: the heirs' outer post, the old stone house on the shore at Blackrose's east edge
what: The stone house caught fire; how it started nobody says.

The heirs keep three bound in the stone house's one room: Says-It-Plain for speaking against them, Hides-In-Reeds for a killing, and Keeps-The-Old-Count, Rows-For-Another's mother, kept at the post working off what the heirs reckon she owes for shelter.

where: outside the stone house's west wall
what: This morning the stone house's way out began burning through; it will bear one more trip out. The heirs' gate-keepers will not go in.

Ussa-Rekh bought out Owings for thirty years and carved a token for each Owing he bought; then he hired out the crews he freed, and keeps a crew's tokens in the chest beside him on the dock until their last season is worked; he promised that a crew who break their tokens before him are done with him.
Heavy-Rope's crew come to Ussa-Rekh to end their last season early, and he refuses them.

when: before the well was dug, and every year since
what: The landing digs its plaster clay at a cut bank where the river swings west below the ford, on the station bank outside its walls. It was the landing's cut before the Imperials came, and the station has never claimed it. The landing renews the clay of its walls every dry season, and its clay work is renewed the same way.

when: the years since the well was dug
what: The Imperials set the well's stone head and lining in the clay bank by the ford. The bank moves with every monsoon, and the lining cracks. Each dry season Livia Varinius re-mortars the cracks herself, with a trowel and a tub of mortar she keeps under the windlass cover. Everyone can see the well head is cracked; nobody at the station knows the lining has cracked and been mended every year. Livia believes a mason's proper new lining will hold where her mortar did not; the lining was Imperial masons' work from the start and has cracked every year since.

when: 5 Rain's Hand, 4E 201 (the ledger page), early this dry season
what: A new crack opens a finger wide from the coping down the lining, on the side that faces the ford, below the water line, beside the old mortar lines. Livia writes it in the station ledger in the old log's order (time, count, state).

Ford water seeps through the lining below ground, and fine silt with it. The morning bucket comes up with silt in the bottom, and the water tastes of the ford. Livia keeps the silt in a jar under the windlass cover, beside her trowel and mortar tub, to show a mason when one comes. She gives a dipper of the well's water to any traveller who has paid the stop.

Livia asks the landing to haul stone for a new lining. Signs-For-The-Cargo refuses. The landing does not build in stone, and it does not drink the well's water; its households draw from the well only to wash.

when: this season, before the ledger page
what: Each bank has always charged for its own half of the stop. Livia raises the station's charge from one drake to two for every traveller who stops, for the stop and its water, to pay a mason from Gideon to re-line the well in stone. She charges the landing's people nothing for water, as she always has.

when: a few days after t5, before 3 Rain's Hand
what: In answer, Signs-For-The-Cargo begins to charge walkers who wade the ford one drake a head; before, only carts on the raft paid. He says the ford was worked before the well was dug. Travellers ask Livia why the landing charges them again, and she writes that in the ledger too.

Some travellers who have paid at the station slip out at night along the station bank, past the clay cut, and wade the shallow tail of the river below the pool, out of the poler's sight, to dodge the landing's charge. They leave prints in the clay of the cut.

when: ten days before the player comes
what: A crocodile, drawn by the offal from the drying racks and the night waders, takes the deep pool under the cut. It comes up at Signs-For-The-Cargo while he digs plaster clay. He drops the clay basket at the cut and runs. Nobody has dug there since. The station house has no watch post and nobody at the station hunts, so the crocodile has been left alone.

when: now, late in the dry season
what: The rains are close. The landing must replaster its walls before them and has no clay. Takes-The-Short-Weight, who judges everything by its water and keeps a bucket of ford water by her door, told the poler the walkers' charge is wrong and is sending travellers to the crocodile; he would not hear it.

when: every dry season, and early this one
what: The poler's wife draws wash water at the well (the ledger page, 4 Rain's Hand). She has watched Livia at the coping with a trowel every dry season, and this season saw her lift the windlass cover and put silt in a jar. She told Takes-The-Short-Weight.
Ahzi-Tal, a Helstrom courier, lodges for one night. Reeh-Shaal, who pays for her bed in salt and travels the same road, sees that his satchel holds a sealed packet his ledger does not list.
Reeh-Shaal buys a length of rope from Tsono-Ra after the lodge has closed, saying she needs it to tie her pack.

Reeh-Shaal kills Ahzi-Tal at the stone lip, takes the satchel, ties the body's wrists and pins it with a grave-stake in the spring's throat under the Hist's roots, so it will not float up. She leaves the stake's face uncarved.
Haj-Tei finds the courier's bed empty, his pack still in the lodge store and his bill unpaid. He decides the courier left before dawn without paying and keeps the pack against the debt.
The body fouls the water. Guests who drink it, or eat food cooked in it, fall sick with fever and retching.
Reeh-Shaal stays at the lodge, saying she waits for a boat to Helstrom. She waits for the packet's buyer, who has not come, and tells the sick guests it is the fire stand's food.
After the lamps are out, Reeh-Shaal goes to the stone lip and looks down into the water for a while, to be sure the body has not come up. Haj-Tei has seen her there from the lodge door.

where: the plank walk on the landing
what: Wuleen-Taza began dumping fish offal in the shallows under the plank walk at night from the crew's bait bucket and spreading word of a beast that took boats in the deep channel, so that traders would hire the crew's rafts and not the boat captain's boat.

where: the shallows under the plank walk
what: The offal drew a real crocodile up the river; it made its lair in the shallows under the plank walk and took a raft and its rafter's catch.
Okan-Zish, afraid of the beast now that it is real, wants it killed and says nothing of the bait.

where: the gate at the city's edge
what: Sei-Wan walked out of the gate into the basin alone, east through the shallows, to prove himself to Helstrom's Agaceph.

where: the roots in the shallows of the basin east of the gate
what: A viper came out of the roots and has kept Sei-Wan pinned among them since.
Haj-Wan waits by the gate; the levy warden will not follow, because the custom of Helstrom's Agaceph forbids its own to trail a walk-out.

where: the lower channel below Nine Bends, then the estuary bank above Lilmoth
what: The months of an Owing gang and their families were sold on from the lower channel to Buys-The-Months, a Lilmoth debt-labour broker, who hires the gang out to unload the lighters at Lilmoth's dock and keeps their months on his work roll. The families lodge at a camp on the estuary bank a night's rowing above Lilmoth, and so as not to wash out far from their tree they planted a cutting of Nine Bends' Hist there, with their clutch at its roots (QA1). Ux-Xeek is his port hand, who calls the gang out to the lighters. Dives-Without-A-Rope, of a family that answers to Nine Bends, has thinned in colour from her years away from it.

Cuts-the-Old-Knot learns that the state's courier, Mee-Tuja, will come down to Lilmoth with the broker's gang from its camp, as cover, carrying a sealed satchel for the Veiled Reed's handler in Lilmoth, and that the camp keeps a small Hist cutting.

where: the gang's camp on the estuary bank
what: Her cell comes in off the water. She kills Mee-Tuja and takes the satchel; two of her people cut the cutting's roots from the clutch and draw its sap into jars they brought; the huts burn and the eggs die. A stranger lies hurt by the fire, on no roll and known to nobody there; she looks at the stranger and leaves them alive. How the stranger came to the bank nobody at the camp knows.

Wuleen-Sei, the broker's overseer, gets the gang into its longboat and down the estuary through the night to the broker's ship, moored at the pier at Hereguard Plantation, west of Lilmoth, where the gang sleeps in the hold. Dives-Without-A-Rope carries the hurt stranger aboard, and a jar one of the cutters dropped by the fire.

Nesh-Deeka waits at the house Salts-The-Catch keeps for the Reed (QA8) for a courier who does not come. When the ship comes in without him, Salts-The-Catch, who sells the broker his gang's food, asks him at the pier for anyone off the ship who saw the camp burn, for whom her guest, Nesh-Deeka, will pay. The broker tells her of the jar and the stranger, and keeps his own hands, who are his months. The broker passes on what his overseer told him: the woman with the knotted cord had the cutting cut from its eggs, and looked at the stranger by the fire and let them live.

The stranger wakes in the hold. Buys-The-Months stands on the pier beside the ship. The stranger's name is on no line of his roll, so they owe him nothing and he cannot hire them out; he wants them off his pier.

when: two nights before the game opens
where: the gang's camp on the estuary bank
what: Two of the cell's people came off the water with empty jars, cut the cutting's roots at the clutch and filled the jars from the cut roots; one jar, filled and stoppered, rolled from a cutter's arm by the fire and was left when the cell went back to the water (MQ01 t2).

Dives-Without-A-Rope, whose family answers to Nine Bends, the cutting's parent, picked up the jar and carried it aboard with the hurt stranger. She keeps it in a lockbox she keeps locked, with the key on her, meaning to lick the sap and hear her tree once before it is taken from her. She has not dared taste it yet; twenty gold would be a month off her roll. Ux-Xeek's spare picks for the lighters' padlocks lie loose on the hold's floor by the lockbox.

Nesh-Deeka, told of the jar by Salts-The-Catch from the broker, sends the Reed's new hand for it. She has heard that sap shows a taster visions, and that a stranger tastes it differently; she means to have the stranger taste it and to write down whatever they say. The same day word reaches her that the Hist of Low-Reed Village, east of Lilmoth, has turned its face.

when: when the player tastes the sap
what: The sap holds the player for some breaths. They speak of the ship's hold, empty, with roots grown up through its deck in a ring like trees, and a door at the top of its stairs that is not the ship's door and that nobody built, and a dry voice in it that makes no words; on a stranger the sap leaves a dry anger that passes (QA18). Nesh-Deeka writes it down and gives the page to the player. What it means stays unexplained (§18d).
Cuts-the-Old-Knot sends two of her cell, Hides-His-Wake and Counts-The-Jars, each with the knotted cord at the wrist, to try the cut-and-draw on a tended Hist with a village round it.

While Pays-Late, the tree-minder, is out on the water with the netters, the two men pole in from the north reeds, take his knife and a pot of his gum from the unbarred sap-workshop, cut a root of the Hist at the ring, draw its sap into jars, seal the cut with the black gum and pole away. The egg-tender sees a boat come and go and takes it for a netter.

The Hist turns its face, its light out and its leaves shut. The cut severs the uxith from the tree and the eggs die of it, so the uxith goes dark. The sap weeping at the cut draws the leech water's leeches to the cut root (QA11).

Pays-Late finds the root cut and sealed with his own gum and his knife gone. Knowing it will look like his work, he tells only the egg-tender, bars the workshop, follows the drips north to the leech water and loses them there, and goes down every night after dark to wash the weeping cut.

The village sees the leeches and blames them, and blames Pays-Late, whose keeping the tree and its water are; it sees him go down to the cut root at night. The root-herald trusts no stranger from Lilmoth.

The two men keep the jars at a camp on a dry rise in the north reeds, past the last stilt house, where the reeds bend, beyond the leech water, waiting for the cell's larger boat; one keeps watch on the trail side. Pays-Late's knife lies by their fire, kept for the next draw.

A root of the village's Hist was cut at the ring for its sap and its clutch died of the cut; the player saw the cut root and the camp where the sap was kept. A Hist that falls silent kills no clutch (hist-and-sap), so the cut is a different thing from the silence.

Nesh-Deeka decides that the interior's tree-minders and Nisswo, who gather at Helstrom and carry news home, must hear what a cut Hist looks like from someone the Reed can deny. She will not send escorts with the player.

where: the landing, the marsh and the gate
what: Two giant wasps keep the way's far bend, over the Heart-Mud, where the way runs over a root; the levy warden at the gate says what the basin does to those who walk into it.

where: the Hall of the Scalded Throne
what: The seat is swept, as it has been swept for years; nobody can say whether it was ever filled.

when: all day, the quarrel in the evening
what: Kaska-Meen keeps her watch in the grove and Ei-Tuja stands at the root's foot, all day; in the evening they quarrel, as they have before, over what a silent Hist means: she holds that it must be watched by tree-minders alone, he that its silence is its own act, to be read and not clamped. Neither has seen a cut root.

In a dry year the founders went down the root galleries and cut a channel from a brine seam toward the roots of a rival grove downstream, to sour its water and take its travellers. The rival grove withered; Greenspring grew.
The founders carved the descent on their own grave-stakes in the old way, as a deed done for the tribe, and never spoke of it to outsiders.
With the grove downstream dead, the channel silted on that side; each flood now pushes the brine back up the cut into Greenspring's own taproots.
Vees-Wai finds the Hist's leaves falling out of season and the sap thin. The village tastes salt in the spring and blames the salt works upstream.
Ixo-Vaal stopped trading for salt-works salt when the works closed their landing; he now buys upriver rock salt, which he keeps in a sack at his door.
S'Tabi sells to the Chapter and sends those who ask the right way to Tilts-The-Jug inside the house.
Keeps-What-Floats took a necklace of polished blue jaspers from another thief of the dock while he slept. He is a coward and runs from any fight.
Tilts-The-Jug decides to see how the newcomer works: the necklace is to come back with no harm done to the one who took it.

Keeps-What-Floats walks the dock and boardwalk by day, drinks with Sits-By-The-Water by the water in the evening and sleeps on a bedroll under the shacks' eaves north-west of the house at night, the necklace on him all the while.
The Chapter's way down is a trapdoor just north of Pusbottom, kept locked; whoever comes down by it has opened it.

where: the deep water north of Pusbottom
what: A merchant's stilt house fell from its rotten stilts onto the floor of the deep water. The merchant's lockbox of pledged things, locked, came to rest beside it in the open. The ripper eels hunt there.
Bent-Spine wants the lockbox up before its clients find a diver, and leaves to the player what becomes of what is in it.
Three clients wait on the bank, each with a claim on one thing in the box, and each claim is a lie.
The figurine is worn smooth by many hands over many years; the merchant had the charm set in a new silver mount of his own; the beads are Kothringi glass, the kind the old cairns hold.
